Book p.386: Atrioventricular Septal Defect

TERMINOLOGY: • Central cardiac defect involving atrial and ventricular
septum, atrioventricular (AV) valves, and conducting system
• AV septal defect can be balanced or unbalanced
○ Balanced defect: Right and left ventricles are equal in
size with equal commitment of AV valves
○ Unbalanced defect: 1 ventricle gets majority of inflow
and is equivalent to single ventricle
• Defect can be complete or partial
○ Partial: Primum atrial septal defect (ASD), distinct mitral
and tricuspid valve anuli, cleft in mitral valve
○ Complete: Primum ASD, contiguous inlet ventricular
septal defect, and common AV valve has single anulus
IMAGING: • Missing crux of heart on 4-chamber view
○ Normally, atrial and ventricular septa meet at crux of
heart, and AV valves are separated into 2 distinct valve
anuli
• Single AV valve makes straight line across heart in systole
○ Identify commitment of AV valve to ventricles
○ Small ventricle suggestive of unbalanced defect
• Defect in primum atrial septum and inlet ventricular
septum
• Gooseneck deformity of left ventricular outflow tract
PATHOLOGY: • Trisomy 21 in up to 50% of fetal cases
• Other chromosomal anomalies or syndromes in 20-30%
CLINICAL ISSUES: • Trisomy 21 not independent risk factor for adverse surgical
outcome
• Excellent short- and long-term surgical outcomes in
liveborns (95% 20-year survival rate)
